Decoder-only transformers reliably route disproportionate attention weight to a small number of early tokens — often the BOS token or the first few content tokens — across nearly all heads and layers, a phenomenon called attention sink formation. The central question is why this happens and what it costs: sinks appear to be a mathematical pressure valve, allowing softmax to dump weight somewhere "safe" when no token is genuinely relevant, but they occupy positions that are also inside the active context window, creating a structural tension between their stabilizing role and their consumption of finite positional budget. Key concepts include the softmax normalization forcing weights to sum to one (which incentivizes sink formation when attention logits are uniformly low), the residual stream as the actual carrier of information (meaning high attention weight ≠ high information flow), rotary or learned positional encodings that give early tokens implicit geometric privilege, and the distinction between local sinks (head-specific) and global sinks (cross-layer, where the same positions are suppressed everywhere). What an expert worries about that a beginner misses is the interaction effect: sinks are not just wasted attention — they actively reshape the effective context by creating a soft boundary that influences how keys and queries at later positions are calibrated, meaning that as context windows stretch to 128K+ tokens, sink behavior can degrade retrieval from the middle of the window in ways that aggregate loss curves will not reveal, because the model still looks competent on average even while specific positional bands become nearly invisible.

When a position functions as a sink across many layers, its residual stream accumulates a distinctive statistical signature: the vector at that position gets written to by many attention heads (each adding its output projection), but the content of those writes is largely uninformative — heads are dumping weight there precisely because they're not extracting meaningful information, so the update vectors tend to cancel or compress into a low-variance attractor state. Nostalgia for the original embedding fades; what remains is something closer to a "sink eigenvector" — a direction in residual stream space that subsequent layers have learned to recognize as the safe target for excess attention weight. This is self-reinforcing because once a position's residual stream stabilizes into this attractor, its key vector (computed from that stream) becomes increasingly well-calibrated to receive attention from query vectors that are uncertain or diffuse — the position essentially advertises itself as a sink through its key geometry. Elhage et al.'s 2021 transformer circuits work is the conceptual ancestor here, showing that residual stream composition is additive and that heads can read "tags" written by earlier heads; sink formation is essentially an emergent tag that says "dump here." Concretely, StreamingLLM (Xiao et al., 2023) exploited exactly this by showing that retaining just the first 4 sink tokens plus a sliding local window preserved perplexity across 4M token sequences — which only makes sense if those positions have a stable, layer-spanning functional role, not a coincidental one. The numbers matter: they found that evicting sink tokens caused perplexity to spike catastrophically (from ~8 to >1000 in LLaMA-2), whereas evicting equivalent non-sink early tokens had almost no effect, confirming the attractor isn't about positional content but about the residual stream state itself.

Direct evidence here is thin — this sits at the frontier where activation steering research and mechanistic interpretability of sinks haven't fully converged — but what we can piece together from adjacent work is instructive. Representation engineering (Zou et al., 2023) and activation addition (Turner et al., 2023) both work by injecting steering vectors into the residual stream at targeted layers; when you do this at a sink position, you're fighting the attractor dynamics directly, because subsequent heads have learned to write toward that attractor state, meaning the intervention gets partially overwritten with each passing layer rather than propagating cleanly forward. The most likely outcome is not collapse but displacement: the sink migrates to the next most geometrically convenient position, typically another early token, because the softmax pressure that created the sink hasn't been removed — you've just destabilized one landing zone, so the system finds another. This is analogous to what happens in StreamingLLM when the true BOS token is absent: the model spontaneously promotes a nearby early token to sink status, suggesting the attractor is a role the architecture needs filled, not a property of any specific token's content. What's particularly non-obvious is that intervention at sink positions might actually harm downstream task performance even if it appears to redirect attention more "usefully," because the sink's role in absorbing diffuse, low-confidence attention weight is stabilizing — removing it without replacing the pressure valve can increase entropy in the attention distributions of middle and late layers, degrading coherence in ways that show up as subtle repetition or topic drift rather than obvious failure.

The evidence strongly suggests that heavy sink-users and in-context retrieval heads are dissociated, not overlapping populations. Olsson et al. (2022) identified induction heads — the primary mechanism for in-context retrieval — as operating via a precise two-head circuit where one head copies previous token positions and another attends back to completions of matching prefixes; these heads produce sharp, targeted attention patterns with low entropy, which is the opposite behavioral signature of sink-heavy heads that produce flat, diffuse distributions with a spike at the sink position. Wang et al.'s IOI (indirect object identification) work similarly found that name-mover heads and key-query heads responsible for fact retrieval operate with high attention specificity, whereas the heads with chronically high sink weight tend to cluster in early-to-middle layers and appear to function more like "residual stream maintenance" heads — keeping the stream well-conditioned for later computation rather than doing content retrieval themselves. The functional interpretation that holds up best is a division of labor: sink-heavy heads are essentially performing a form of attention dropout by design, preventing their output projections from writing noise into the residual stream when no genuine pattern is present, while retrieval heads reserve their capacity for sharp pattern-matching. What's concretely worrying for long-context systems is that this dissociation means you can't easily identify sink overuse by monitoring retrieval head behavior — a model can have perfectly healthy induction and name-mover heads while simultaneously having its sink-heavy heads consuming positional budget in ways that crowd out the queries that retrieval heads need to find their targets, particularly in the 4K–32K range where positional encodings begin to decorrelate and retrieval heads start missing matches that sink-heavy heads have effectively buried.

Attention-score-based KV cache pruning schemes — H2O (Zhang et al., 2023) being the canonical example — compute importance by accumulating attention weight each token has received across heads and layers, then evict low-scoring entries. The fatal flaw this dissociation exposes is that sink-heavy heads inflate the scores of sink positions enormously while retrieval heads, which attend sharply but infrequently (they fire precisely when a match exists, not continuously), contribute relatively little to the cumulative score of the tokens they actually need. The result is a systematic bias: sink positions are virtually never evicted (correctly, as StreamingLLM showed), but the retrieval targets — the specific content tokens that induction or name-mover heads will need to attend back to — accumulate low scores during the long stretches when no retrieval is happening, making them look expendable right up until the moment they're critical. H2O reported 20x compression with modest perplexity degradation on standard benchmarks, but those benchmarks don't stress delayed retrieval — the pathological case is a key fact mentioned at position 8K in a 32K context that no head attends to until position 30K, at which point it's already been evicted because its cumulative attention score never crossed the retention threshold. SnapKV (Li et al., 2024) partially addressed this by using the query at the current decoding step to prospectively identify which KV entries will matter, rather than retrospectively scoring by past attention — but this only helps when the relevant query has already been issued, failing for multi-hop retrieval where the model doesn't know it needs a fact until after a reasoning step that hasn't happened yet. The positions most likely to be incorrectly evicted are therefore not random middle-context tokens but specifically: low-frequency entities, numerical values, and clause-initial tokens that carry propositional content but receive sparse attention during the encoding pass.

The residual stream does carry anticipatory signals, and there's meaningful evidence this isn't just theoretical. Geva et al. Practically, this means a lightweight probe trained on mid-layer residual stream activations at the current decoding position could, in principle, predict which key positions are about to receive high attention weight from retrieval heads 3-6 layers before those heads actually execute — giving a prospective protection signal without needing to wait for the attention pattern to materialize. Nothing in production systems currently exploits this, but the mechanistic scaffolding is there: lookahead decoding work (Fu et al., 2023) and speculative decoding both demonstrate that future-state prediction from intermediate residual representations is tractable, and the retrieval precursor problem is structurally similar. The harder obstacle is that multi-hop retrieval chains — where the output of one retrieval operation becomes the query for the next — would require iterative prospective protection, and the second hop's target is genuinely uncomputable from the residual stream before the first hop resolves, creating an irreducible blind spot that no single-pass anticipatory scheme can close. What makes this concretely promising for near-term systems is that single-hop retrieval, which covers the majority of factual recall tasks, may be protectable with a probe adding less than 1% inference overhead if it operates only on the last-token residual stream at selected middle layers rather than the full KV cache scoring pass.

Partial retrieval does produce systematic bias, and the direction is predictable: when the residual stream carries a mix of retrieved and unretieved components, MLP layers pattern-complete by collapsing the ambiguity toward the highest-frequency completion conditioned on the retrieved fragment, which means errors cluster around plausible-but-wrong neighbors in the model's implicit knowledge graph rather than random noise. Meng et al.'s ROME and MEMIT work (2022-2023) is relevant here because their causal tracing revealed that factual associations are stored in middle-layer MLP weights as key-value pairs, and partial retrieval effectively activates the key without fully resolving the value — the resulting MLP output is a weighted blend of multiple value vectors, and the blend systematically favors whichever value has stronger weight-space representation, typically the more frequent or more recently reinforced association. This means partial retrieval errors are coherent rather than random: a model partially retrieving a biographical fact will tend to substitute attributes from the most similar high-frequency entity rather than producing an obviously broken output, which is exactly why confabulation is hard to catch with surface-level fluency metrics. The correction problem without ground truth is tractable in limited ways: Chuang et al.'s DoLa (2023) showed that contrasting logit distributions between early and late layers amplifies the retrieved signal over the pattern-completion signal, because early layers haven't yet collapsed the ambiguity — subtracting early-layer predictions from late-layer predictions suppresses the high-frequency prior bleed-through and improves factual accuracy by 10-20% on TruthfulQA-style benchmarks without any external knowledge. The fundamental limit is that correction schemes like DoLa or inference-time intervention can amplify whatever retrieval signal exists but cannot manufacture a retrieval signal that isn't there — so for facts where the retrieved fragment is too sparse to discriminate between candidate completions, the bias toward high-frequency neighbors remains after correction, just with lower confidence scores that at least signal the uncertainty rather than hiding it.
